Q: Division and floating points A:

The problem is integer truncation .. you are dividing two integers => the result will be another integer with the fractional part thrown away. (So for instance in the case when the real result of an integer division would be 3.9, truncation would make it 3 (ie. it doesn't round)).

In your case, if you change this to:

x2 = 360 / 4095.0;  /* one of the operands now has a decimal point */

you'll get

0.087912, 0.087912

as output.

I.e., as soon as one or both of the operands of the division operator / are float/doubles, the result will be too (i.e., it will be "promoted" to float/double). So I could have changed x2 to

x2 = 360.0 / 4095.0;

or

x2 = 360.0 / 4095;

and would have gotten the same result as above.

As mentioned by @chris just using a . is sufficient too.

Re your question above about precision:

You are already working with long doubles .. I don't think internally you can change anything unless you use some special library, but you can certainly display more digits. E.g., 

  printf("%Lf, %.20Lf \n",x1, x2);

will yield 

  0.087912, 0.08791208791208791895

Finally, as @edA-qa mort-ora-y reminds us, you can also cast values to certain types, but it matters when you do it. A simple example (note that the values end up as float after the assignment in any case since v is a float):

float v = 0;
                     /* values shown are BEFORE assignment */
v = (5 / 2);         /* value is 2 due to integer truncation before assignment */
v = (float) (5 / 2); /* 2.0 as integer division occurs 1st, then cast to float */
v = (float) 5 / 2;   /* 2.5 since 5 becomes 5.0 through casting first. */

Q: Addition without Operators A:

Let's pretend that we are doing 12 + 43. Computers often stores these as binary, so it becomes 1102 + 1010112 (subscript 2 means binary). Think about normal carry over addition. We will pad with some zeroes:

    000110

    101011

+_________

By adding them together, and doing carry overs where neccessary, we can find our answer to be 1101112. Computers achieve this by going from right to left, maintaining a carry-over value and using logic gates. You can read this for details.

Q: Can someone help decoding a mingw32 error? A:

On some further checking I believe the cause is this macro: https://github.com/Rhekar/CCCaster/blob/master/targets/DllAsmHacks.hpp#L86-L90

#define INLINE_DWORD(X)                                                         \
    static_cast<unsigned char> ( unsigned ( X ) & 0xFF ),                       \
    static_cast<unsigned char> ( ( unsigned ( X ) >> 8 ) & 0xFF ),              \
    static_cast<unsigned char> ( ( unsigned ( X ) >> 16 ) & 0xFF ),             \
    static_cast<unsigned char> ( ( unsigned ( X ) >> 24 ) & 0xFF )

Specific when it's invoked like this: https://github.com/Rhekar/CCCaster/blob/master/targets/DllAsmHacks.hpp#L587

0xE8, INLINE_DWORD ( ( ( char * ) &addExtraTexturesCb ) - 0x41BE38 - 5 ),       // call addExtraTexturesCb

I guess all the nested parens and casts is confusing mingw to think this is an array of functions somehow.

How to resolve this is still an issue, but I guess the question of "what's causing the error" is solved.

Q: librtlsdr.dll - vs2026 won't let me add the librtlsdr.dll file A:

librtlsdr.dll is a native DLL library which is intended to be called by C programs, not C# or any .Net binaries directly. That's why there's a wrapper package for .Net called "RtlSdrManager", which eventually calls librtlsdr.dll to do the actual work. According to its on-line document:

NuGet Gallery | RtlSdrManager 0.7.1

Its "Prerequisites" section explains:

The librtlsdr native library must be installed on the system

The recommended way suggested in the document is:

choco install rtl-sdr

On the other hand, Microsoft provides an official document explaining how .Net binaries search for the native DLL files:

Dynamic-link library search order - Win32 apps | Microsoft Learn

So there's another easy way is to go with its item #7:

  1. The folder the calling process was loaded from (the executable's folder)

Which means you can achieve it by following these steps:

  1. In your project source code folder, you need to manually copy the downloaded librtlsdr.dll file to where you keep the project's C# source code.
  2. Start Visual Studio, edit the project's property, open the "Build" -> "Events" tab on the left panel.
  3. In the "Pre-build event" box on the right panel, write a simple DOS "copy" command to copy that DLL file to the build output folder. Since the output folder will be different among various build configurations ("release", "debug", etc), you cannot write fixed folder path in that box. The command should be: copy "$(ProjectDir)librtlsdr.dll" "$(TargetDir)"

See also: Specify build events (C#)

Q: Getting response %40 in place of @ how should i convert it A:

You can use urldecode();

echo urldecode("%40"); // @

Q: How can I extract the decimal part from a floating point number in C? A:

My printf() didn't support formatting for floats. This was my solution to print it as two integers. Change 100 in to what you like to increase the precision.

I found this one:

#define DEC(f) (uint32_t)(100*((f)-(float)((uint32_t)(f))))
#define INT(f) (uint32_t)(f)

DEC(3.1416..) = 14 (int) 
INT(3.1416..) = 3 (int)

Q: Which is the better way to calculate the size of one array in a for statement? A:

The generally recommended practice is that you get the count once and store it in a variable before the start of the loop (the first section of for loop). This prevents "extended" looping by mutating the array during iteration and is slightly better for performance (as of PHP 7.2, the difference is too small with arrays to be of importance for anything).

However, most people prefer to iterate over an array with foreach, which is a better choice in almost every way, except for performance. For 99.99% of the tasks, you should not be concerned with which one is faster, as their performance is so negligible that it would only make a difference if you had millions of them in your code. So for most taks you should prefer this:

foreach ($array as $element) {

}

Regarding performance: for($i = 0, $size = count($array); $i < $size; ++$i){ ... } is about 5% faster than for($i = 0; $i < count($array); ++$i){ ... } on average, but that depends on several factors. Two main factors are: whether you are on PHP 7.2+ and whether count() is fully qualified (when inside a namespace, use \count()). If that's not the case, you could even see 20% difference in performance, but all of that is useless numbers because this function is so fast that it does not matter which one you use unless you are taking part in some extreme performance challenge.

count() does not count the elements in the array each time it is called! It only returns the number of elements in the array hashtable which is O(1) operation.

Q: How to configure SonarQube for Typescript based AngularJS project? A:

I think your lcov.info path is wrong in your sonar-project.properties. This is mine:

# TypeScript specific config
sonar.typescript.lcov.reportPaths=coverage/my-project/lcov.info
sonar.test.inclusions=**/*.spec.ts

Q: java mongodb driver how do you catch exceptions? A:

You can redirect System.err to a ByteArrayOutputStream buffer. If a runtime exception is thrown, it will be collected into the buffer. See an answer to a similar problem at: https://stackoverflow.com/a/47699292/7388679
